idiom_name: nil for optional parameters, minimal empty conformance for non-optional ones
implementation_notes: Swift distinguishes optional from non-optional types at compile time: a parameter declared Collaborator? takes nil as the placeholder, while a non-optional protocol parameter needs an instance, and the cheapest is a small struct or final class in the test target whose conformance has empty bodies (a test-local extension of an existing dummy type works too). Swift models the absent value as the .none case of the Optional enum rather than as a null pointer, so nil is a language value with pattern-matching semantics. Third-party mock generators fabricate protocol doubles, but their default behaviour is stubbing rather than inertness, so they belong to the configurable-double family. Discarding an ignored argument is written _ or `_ =` on the callee side.
pitfalls: fatalError() or try! inside a dummy conformance turns the placeholder into a crash when the path changes - deliberate as a fail-fast guard, dangerous as an unmarked dummy.

An empty struct conformance is value-typed: a protocol that does not constrain Self to AnyObject mutates a copy through the interface, so recording state on a struct-shaped dummy silently records nothing.
Forcing production APIs to accept Collaborator? just so tests can pass nil leaks a test convenience into the interface; a small conformance keeps the signature honest.
